title: Lamellarization–tempering induced heterogeneous lamellar structures achieving strength–toughness synergy in HSLA steel
abstract: Abstract Achieving a favorable strength–toughness balance in thick-section low-alloy steels remains a critical challenge for structural applications. The effects of lamellarization annealing (L) and subsequent tempering (T) temperatures on microstructural evolution and mechanical performance were systematically examined in a 30-mm-thick thermo-mechanical controlled processing plate. The L temperature was varied from 800 to 860 °C, followed by T at 400–550 °C. Microstructural evolution was characterized using optical microscopy, scanning electron microscopy, electron backscatter diffraction, and X-ray diffraction (XRD), while tensile and Charpy V-notch impact tests were conducted to evaluate mechanical performance. Lower L temperatures (800 and 820 °C) promoted the formation of heterogeneous lamellar structures composed of martensite/bainite and intercritical ferrite. This microstructural heterogeneity enhanced plastic deformation capability and low-temperature impact toughness by increasing the density of high-angle grain boundaries and promoting favorable dislocation configurations. In contrast, higher L temperatures (840 and 860 °C) led to microstructural homogenization and dislocation accumulation, which improved strength but significantly deteriorated toughness. T at 400 °C resulted in insufficient recovery and limited toughness improvement. An optimal strength–toughness balance was achieved at 500 °C, whereas T at 550 °C caused over-recovery, leading to a slight reduction in toughness despite enhanced ductility. XRD analysis revealed that a high fraction of screw dislocations combined with a moderate dislocation density enhanced crack-tip plasticity and ductile fracture behavior. The L 810 T 500  condition (810 °C represents an intermediate L temperature within the optimal range of 800–820 °C) achieved the best synergy: tensile strength ~900 MPa, elongation of more than 17%, and impact toughness of more than 250 J at −40 °C.
journal: Journal of Iron and Steel Research International

sections.heading: Introduction
paragraphs: High-strength low-alloy (HSLA) steels are widely used in structural applications such as bridges, ships, and cryogenic vessels due to their high strength, good low-temperature toughness, and weldability [ 1 ,  2 – 3 ]. Demanding cryogenic environments further require improved toughness and reliability. However, the inherent trade-off between strength and toughness remains a key obstacle in alloy design [ 4 ].

The conventional quenching (Q) and tempering (T) process improves strength mainly through martensitic transformation and precipitation strengthening. Yet, the high defect density and residual stresses in quenched martensite hinder crack blunting and may lead to brittle fracture at low temperatures [ 5 ]. Previous studies have shown that a proper fraction of retained austenite (RA) can enhance toughness via the transformation-induced plasticity (TRIP) effect [ 6 ], while excessive RA reduces yield strength [ 7 ]. Therefore, optimizing the strength–toughness balance is a key approach to improving the low-temperature performance of HSLA steels.

The quenching–lamellarization–tempering (QLT) process has recently shown promise for improving cryogenic toughness, particularly in Ni-rich steels [ 8 ]. Direct quenching (DQ) also refines microstructures and combining DQ with lamellarization annealing (L) and T offers an effective approach to strength–toughness synergy [ 9 ,  10 ]. The QLT process consists of quenching, lamellarization in the (α + γ) region, and tempering [ 6 ]. The fraction of reversed austenite is controlled by L temperature and holding time [ 11 ], while its formation and growth kinetics are dominated by carbon diffusion and element partitioning [ 12 ,  13 ,  14 – 15 ]. Upon Q, the reversed austenite transforms into martensite/bainite (M/B) while intercritical ferrite (IF) remains as a soft phase [ 16 ]. Subsequent T promotes carbon redistribution and carbide precipitation, relieving residual stress and enabling dislocation recovery [ 17 ]. These processes together produce a refined multiphase microstructure that enhances low-temperature toughness without compromising strength [ 18 ].

Although the QLT process has proven effective in improving toughness in Ni-rich and microalloyed steels, systematic studies on its application to HSLA structural steels are still limited. Existing studies have rarely provided a comprehensive understanding of how L and T temperatures synergistically influence the microstructure–property relationship. In particular, the interaction among IF, heterogeneous microstructures, and dislocation states is still not fully understood, hindering a full understanding of the QLT process in HSLA steels.

In this study, HSLA steel was treated by varying lamellarization (800–860 °C) and T (350–550 °C) temperatures to clarify their effects on microstructure and mechanical properties. Characterization showed that localized austenitization generates size heterogeneity; after Q, ultrafine M/B forms within coarser laths, producing a heterogeneous lamellar structure that differs from the film-like RA typical of conventional QLT [ 19 ]. These insights support the optimization of QLT processing for improved strength–toughness synergy.

sections.heading: Material and processing
paragraphs: The tested HSLA steel (C 0.07, Mn 1.6, Cu 0.4, Si 0.3, (Ni + Cr + Mo) 1.7, Nb 0.04, Ti 0.015, and Fe balance, in wt.%) was produced by vacuum induction melting. The thermo-mechanical controlled processing (TMCP) route (Fig.  1 a) consisted of homogenization at 1220 °C for 2 h, followed by rough rolling at 1000–1050 °C with a 50% thickness reduction. Finish rolling was then performed at 800–850 °C with an additional 60% reduction. Immediately after rolling, accelerated cooling (ACC) was applied at 20–30 °C/s to 400 °C, followed by air cooling (AC) to room temperature. The specimens then underwent L and T treatments. During the L stage, reheating and holding promoted reversed austenite formation before water quenching (WQ). The subsequent T stage relieved internal stresses and optimized the strength–toughness balance, followed by AC. Fig. 1 Schematic diagram of heat treatment routes ( a ) and dilatometric curves measured during double quenching to obtain critical transformation temperature of experimental steel plate ( b )

The effects of L and T temperatures on microstructure and mechanical properties were investigated using 30-mm-thick TMCP plates. Charpy V-notch (CVN) impact specimens were taken parallel to the rolling direction, while tensile specimens were machined perpendicular to it.

A dilatometric test (DIL 805A, BAHR-Thermoanalyse GmbH, Germany) was performed to determine the critical transformation temperatures ( A c1 ,  A c3 , and  M s ). The specimen was heated to 1150 °C at 10 °C/s and cooled to room temperature at 30 °C/s (Fig.  1 b). According to the dilatometric results, the L and T temperature ranges were set to 800–860 and 350–550 °C, with holding time of 40 and 60 min, respectively. To isolate individual parameters, the T temperature was fixed at 350 °C when studying the effect of L temperature (L 800 T 350 , L 820 T 350 , L 840 T 350 , L 860 T 350 ), and the L temperature was fixed at 810 °C (representing an intermediate L temperature within the optimal range of 800–820 °C) when studying the effect of T temperature (L 810 T 400,  L 810 T 500,  L 810 T 550 ).

sections.heading: Microstructure characterization and mechanical property testing
paragraphs: Optical microscopy (OM, Axio Vert.A1, ZEISS, Germany) and scanning electron microscopy (SEM, Auriga, ZEISS, Germany; 20 keV, 15 mm working distance) were used to examine the microstructures at the surface (S) and mid-thickness (R) on the rolling direction–normal direction (RD–ND) plane. Specimens were mechanically polished and etched with 4% Nital before observation.

Specimens for X-ray diffraction (XRD) and electron backscatter diffraction (EBSD) were mechanically ground and polished, followed by electro-polishing in a 6 vol.% perchloric acid-alcohol solution at 20 V for 15 s. XRD analyses were conducted over a diffraction angle (2 θ ) range of 40°–120° with a step size of 0.02° and a scanning speed of 2 (°)/min. Measurements were performed on a Rigaku DMAX-RB diffractometer (Rigaku Corporation, Tokyo, Japan) operated at 40 kV and 150 mA using Cu Kα radiation (X-ray wavelength  λ  = 0.15406 nm) with a graphite monochromator.

EBSD analysis was conducted with a step size of 0.3 μm using an SEM equipped with an HKL Symmetry S2 detector (Oxford Instruments, UK). The acquired orientation data were processed using AztecCrystal software (Oxford HKL). Kernel average misorientation (KAM) was evaluated to quantify local strain. Grain boundaries with misorientations of 2°–15° were classified as low-angle grain boundaries (LAGBs), and those above 15° as high-angle grain boundaries (HAGBs) [ 1 ]. The relative grain boundary density, defined as the total boundary length per unit area, was used to characterize the evolution of boundary character distribution.

sections.heading: Mechanical properties testing
paragraphs: Round tensile specimens with a gauge length of 30 mm and a testing diameter of 5 mm were machined parallel to the rolling direction. Uniaxial tensile tests were carried out at room temperature on a universal testing machine under a strain rate of 0.001 s −1 . For each condition, three specimens were tested to determine the average mechanical properties.

The CVN impact tests were performed on specimens measuring 10 mm × 10 mm × 55 mm at −40 °C using a 450 J instrumented pendulum impact tester. The V-notch direction was oriented parallel to the transverse direction of the steel plate.

Vickers microhardness measurements across different thickness positions were performed on a SHIMADZU HMV-31ST tester (Japan) under a load of 4.9 N and a dwell time of 15 s. Hardness values were obtained from eight distinct locations and averaged to minimize experimental error.

sections.heading: Effect of L and T temperatures on microstructure
paragraphs: The baseline microstructure of the experimental steel under the TMCP condition is presented in Fig.  2 . Both the S and R regions exhibit comparable microstructural features, mainly composed of M/B laths with a relatively uniform morphology. The laths within packets are fine and well aligned, and a relatively high density of both LAGB (0.79 μm −1 ) and HAGB (1.06 μm −1 ) is observed. In addition, the average KAM value is 1.30°, indicating a high level of stored deformation energy. This boundary-rich microstructure is used as a reference for subsequent L and T treatments. Fig. 2 Characterization results of TMCP state.  a ,  d  OM microstructure of experimental steel at surface and mid-thickness;  b ,  e  SEM microstructure of experimental steel at surface and mid-thickness;  c ,  f  inverse pole figures (IPF) maps and KAM maps at mid-thickness

Compared with the TMCP state, varying the L temperature (800–860 °C) followed by T at 350 °C induces pronounced changes in microstructural morphology (Figs.  3  and  4 ). At lower L temperatures (800 and 820 °C), the microstructure consists of M/B and IF, with necklace-like ultrafine grains dispersed among coarse lath regions. As the L temperature increases to 840 and 860 °C, the fraction of IF decreases and the necklace-like structure gradually disappears, leading to a coarser and more uniform M/B microstructure. A homogenized M/B structure is obtained at the highest L temperatures. In order to quantify the evolution of IF with L temperature, the IF area fraction at the mid-thickness region was estimated based on OM using ImageJ, assisted by EBSD band contrast (BC) maps. The IF fraction decreases monotonically with increasing L temperature, from 27% at L 800 T 350  to 16.68% at L 820 T 350  and further to 6.10% at L 840 T 350 . At L 860 T 350 , the IF content is extremely limited and cannot be reliably quantified. Fig. 3 OM microstructure of experimental steel at surface ( a – d ) and mid-thickness ( e – h ) lamellarized at different annealing temperatures.  a ,  e  800 °C;  b ,  f  820 °C;  c ,  g  840 °C;  d ,  h  860 °C Fig. 4 SEM microstructure of experimental steel at surface ( a – d ) and mid-thickness ( e – h ) lamellarized at different annealing temperatures.  a ,  e  800 °C;  b ,  f  820 °C;  c ,  g  840 °C;  d ,  h  860 °C

As shown in Fig.  5 , the EBSD results indicate that the lower L temperatures (800–820 °C) exhibit clear grain-size heterogeneity, whereas higher temperatures produce more uniform and coarser grains. The KAM values at different L temperatures are 0.69°, 0.71°, 0.90°, and 0.90°, respectively. The corresponding relative grain boundary densities show that the LAGB densities are 0.54, 0.48, 0.53 and 0.47 μm −1 , whereas the HAGB densities are 0.73, 0.73, 0.61, and 0.47 μm −1 , respectively. Fig. 5 IPF maps ( a – d ), KAM maps ( e – h ), and grain boundary misorientation distributions ( i – l ) of experimental steel at various lamellarization annealing temperatures.  a ,  e ,  i  800 °C;  b ,  f ,  j  820 °C;  c ,  g ,  k  840 °C;  d ,  h ,  l  860 °C

At a constant L temperature of 810 °C, varying the T temperatures from 400 to 550 °C induces clear changes in IF distribution and lath morphology (Figs.  6  and  7 ). At 400 °C, abundant IF forms along prior austenite grain boundaries (PAGBs) and lath boundaries. At higher T temperatures (500 and 550 °C), the IF becomes finer and more uniformly dispersed, while the fraction of transformed austenite increases. Fig. 6 OM microstructure of experimental steel at surface ( a – c ) and mid-thickness ( d – f ) tempered at different temperatures.  a ,  c  400 °C;  b ,  d  500 °C;  e ,  f  550 °C Fig. 7 SEM microstructure of experimental steel at surface ( a – c ) and mid-thickness ( d – f ) tempered at different temperatures.  a ,  d  400 °C;  b ,  e  500 °C;  c ,  f  550 °C

As shown in Fig.  8 , EBSD analysis reveals that in the L 810 T 400  sample, certain regions retain the lath arrangement characteristic of the TMCP condition, with only a slight change in lath size (compared with Fig.  2 d). In contrast, L 810 T 500  and L 810 T 550  samples exhibit pronounced lath/bundle coarsening. The KAM values at different T temperatures are 1.04°, 0.94°, and 0.97°, respectively. The corresponding densities of LAGB are 0.64, 0.53, and 0.58 μm −1 , whereas those of HAGB are 0.91, 0.76, and 0.77 μm −1 , respectively. Fig. 8 IPF maps ( a – c ), KAM maps ( d – f ) and grain boundary misorientation distributions ( g – i ) of experimental steel at various tempering temperatures.  a ,  d ,  g  400 °C;  b ,  e ,  h  500 °C;  c ,  f ,  i  550 °C
Overall, L and T treatments modify IF distribution, lath morphology, and boundary characteristics in a consistent and progressive manner.

sections.heading: Effect of L and T temperatures on mechanical properties
paragraphs: In the TMCP state, the steel exhibits relatively high strength (yield strength (YS): 717 MPa at S, 689 MPa at R; tensile strength (TS): 966 MPa at S, 814 MPa at R) but limited ductility, particularly at S, where the total elongation ( e f ) is only 12.7%. The low-temperature toughness is also poor, with the −40 °C CVN impact energy measuring only 46 J (total impact absorbed energy,  W t ) at S, compared with 87 J at R. These properties, together with the relatively homogeneous M/B microstructure, are used as a baseline for assessing the effects of subsequent heat treatments. The tensile properties and CVN impact toughness results at different L temperatures are presented in Fig.  9  and summarized in Table  1 . Fig. 9 Influence of lamellarization annealing temperature on tensile properties ( a ) and impact absorbed toughness ( b ) of experimental steels Table 1 Mechanical properties and phase composition of experimental steel under various L temperatures No. YS/MPa TS/MPa YS/TS ratio e f /% Hardness/HV W t /J Phase L 800 T 350 -S 733 955 0.77 17.43 334 229 TM/B + IF L 800 T 350 -R 741 958 0.77 16.63 348 274 TM/B + IF L 820 T 350 -S 724 947 0.76 16.77 358 252 TM/B + IF L 820 T 350 -R 728 951 0.77 19.12 335 266 TM/B + IF L 840 T 350 -S 819 1012 0.81 12.88 372 36 TM/B L 840 T 350 -R 816 1017 0.80 14.71 368 44 TM/B + IF L 860 T 350 -S 838 1016 0.82 10.35 369 123 TM/B L 860 T 350 -R 851 1021 0.83 3.49 368 34 TM/B Phase—Phase composition of experimental steel; TM/B—tempered martensite/bainite

As illustrated in Fig.  9 a, the S and R positions exhibit nearly identical mechanical responses under most L conditions, except at L 860 T 350  where the S position shows a pronounced loss of ductility and toughness. With T fixed at 350 °C, the effect of L temperature can be categorized into two regimes. At lower L temperatures (800 and 820 °C), the steel exhibits slightly reduced strength but markedly improved ductility and impact toughness, along with low YS/TS ratios (0.76–0.78). As L increases to 840 and 860 °C, both tensile and yield strengths rise steadily (by 5.9% and 12.0% at S and by 11.8% and 14.8% at R), whereas ductility and low-temperature toughness deteriorate sharply. The corresponding increase in YS/TS ratio to 0.81–0.83 indicates a transition toward strength-dominated behavior with diminished plastic reserve. As shown in Fig.  9 b, the −40 °C CVN energy ( W t ) remains high for both positions at L 800 T 350  and L 820 T 350  (all exceeding 220 J), with the maximum value achieved at L 800 T 350 -R (274 J). A sharp deterioration appears once L exceeds 840 °C, with  W t  decreasing to 123 J (S) and 34 J (R) at L 860 T 350 . Overall, increasing L temperature enhances strength and hardness but markedly reduces ductility and toughness. An L temperature of 820 °C provides the most favorable balance of mechanical performance and through-thickness uniformity.

The effect of T temperature was examined using specimens with L at 810 °C in the two-phase region, followed by T at 400–550 °C. The results are presented in Fig.  10  and Table  2 . At 400 °C, the strength remains comparable to that of the TMCP state (YS: 686–687 MPa; TS: 863–869 MPa), while  e f  improves (17.9% for S, 18.8% for R) and toughness increases to 57 (S) and 143 J (R). However, the pronounced toughness gradient between S and R remains. At 500 °C, the steel exhibits the most balanced combination of properties. Yield strength increases to 760 (S) and 756 MPa (R), while tensile strength reaches 903 (S) and 895 MPa (R). The  e f  stays high (17.6%–17.8%), and toughness reaches 225 (S) and 253 J (R). The minimal difference between the two locations indicates good through-thickness uniformity. Further T at 550 °C results in over-tempering, causing a moderate strength reduction (YS: 737–745 MPa; TS: 833–841 MPa), while  e f  slightly increases (19.7% at S and 20.2% at R). Toughness remains high at S (225 J) but decreases slightly at R (215 J), likely due to carbide coarsening or dislocation recovery. Fig. 10 Influence of tempering temperature on tensile properties ( a ) and impact toughness ( b ) of experimental steels Table 2 Mechanical properties and phase composition of experimental steel under various temperatures No. YS/MPa TS/MPa YS/TS ratio e f /% Hardness/HV W t /J Phase L 810 T 400 -S 686 869 0.79 17.90 317 57 TM/B + IF L 810 T 400 -R 687 863 0.80 18.75 295 143 TM/B + IF L 810 T 500 -S 760 903 0.84 17.58 313 225 TM/B + IF L 810 T 500 -R 756 895 0.84 17.78 309 253 TM/B + IF L 810 T 550 -S 737 833 0.88 19.71 303 225 TM/B + IF L 810 T 550 -R 745 841 0.89 20.16 288 215 TM/B + IF

The variation in L temperature appears to influence the strength–toughness relationship mainly through changes in the extent of reversed austenitization, while the T temperature further adjusts this balance via T. Among the tested conditions, lamellarization at 820 °C followed by T at 500 °C yielded the most favorable combination of strength, ductility, and toughness, with minimal variation through the thickness.

sections.heading: Evolution of dislocation state under different L and T temperatures revealed by XRD
paragraphs: Rietveld refinement provided  q  and  d  for the MWH analysis, from which  f screw  was calculated. As shown in Figs.  12 a and  13 a, the  f screw  decreased markedly with an increase in L temperature, from 0.556/0.560 at L 800 T 350  and L 820 T 350  to 0.256/0.289 at L 840 T 350  and L 860 T 350 , indicating that lower L temperatures favor the retention of screw-type dislocations. The  f screw  also declined with higher T temperatures, although L 810 T 400  still exhibited the highest value (0.755), yet with inferior toughness compared with L 810 T 500  and L 810 T 550 . Fig. 12 (Δ K  − 0.9/ d ) 2 / K 2  versus  H 2  ( a ) and MWH plots ( b ) of experimental steel at different lamellarization annealing temperatures (800–860 °C) Fig. 13 (Δ K  − 0.9/ d ) 2 / K 2  versus  H 2  ( a ) and MWH plots ( b ) of experimental steel at different tempering temperatures (400–550 °C)

ρ M , obtained from the MWH fitting (Figs.  12 b and  13 b), first decreased and then slightly increased with rising L temperature. Increasing T temperature led to larger  d  and consequently lower  ρ M ; L 810 T 500  exhibited a  ρ M  of 5.68 × 10 14  m −2 , slightly higher than L 810 T 400 . Overall, both L and T treatments reduce  f screw  and  ρ M  relative to the TMCP condition, which retains a higher  ρ M  and moderate  f screw  due to deformation accumulation during controlled rolling.

sections.heading: Effect of lamellarization annealing temperature
paragraphs: EBSD analysis (Fig.  5 ) reveals that samples treated at 800–820 °C exhibit higher toughness, mainly due to the increased HAGB density and reduced KAM, which enhance crack blunting and strain accommodation [ 1 ,  27 ]. This behavior is also related to phase transformation during L. Austenite primarily nucleates at grain boundaries (model I) and lath interfaces (model II) during L process (Fig.  14 ), especially in alloy-enriched boundary regions [ 12 ,  13 ,  14 – 15 ]. Upon Q, the reversed austenite transforms into necklace-like distributed M/B (Fig.  4 ). T further produces tempered M/B with high dislocation density and fine carbides, improving crack resistance. Unreversed IF mainly undergoes recovery during T, leading to local softening. Fig. 14 Austenite nucleation sites during reverse phase transformation (lamellarization annealing).  a  Nucleation model I;  b  nucleation model II

From the perspective of austenitization kinetics, the effect of L temperature is primarily dictated by the degree of austenitization. At 800 and 820 °C ( A c3  = 861 °C), partial austenitization retains IF and forms transformed M/B. Following T, the fine M/B transforms into TM/B, while IF functions as the soft phase, jointly leading to the formation of a heterogeneous lamellar structure (HLS) [ 28 ,  29 ,  30 ,  31 – 32 ]. This HLS, together with the layered dislocation architecture at heterogeneous interfaces, enhances strain compatibility and energy dissipation near crack tips, thereby lowering ductile-to-brittle transition temperature (DBTT) and improving the strength–toughness balance [ 29 ,  30 ,  31 – 32 ]. The heterogeneity of this lamellar structure is further evidenced by the pronounced disparity in PAGB size revealed by EBSD reconstruction. At 800 and 820 °C, the fine-grained PAG exhibits an average size of ~6.3 μm, whereas the coarse-grained PAG reaches ~42.5 μm, confirming a typical necklace-like grain structure. As the L temperature increases to 840 and 860 °C, enhanced austenitization leads to the dissolution of the heterogeneous lamellar structure, accompanied by an increase in effective grain size and a higher proportion of bainite (Figs.  3  and  4 ). Correspondingly, the overall grain-size distribution becomes more uniform, with the coarse PAG size decreasing to ~21.22 and ~25.05 μm, respectively. At these higher L temperatures, the original rolling-induced PAG morphology is largely eliminated, and the microstructure is predominantly governed by the reverse-transformed austenite during lamellarization rather than by a typical necklace-like grain structure. This evolution indicates a transition toward microstructural homogenization. As a consequence, these microstructural changes collectively reduce the capacity for strain accommodation and crack-tip plasticity, thereby leading to a deterioration in low-temperature toughness.

Although present in a limited fraction, IF remains crucial for crack resistance by enabling local plastic accommodation between hard phases, mitigating stress concentration, and facilitating geometrically necessary dislocation (GND) accumulation, which enhances strain partitioning and strengthens the synergy between strength and toughness [ 33 ,  34 – 35 ]. As the L temperature rises to 840 and 860 °C, the degree of austenitization increases, leading to the progressive disappearance of IF and a corresponding increase in bainitic transformation (Fig.  3 ). Meanwhile, as the fraction of bainite increases, the overall HAGB density decreases, which promotes crack propagation and consequently causes cleavage fracture and a significant drop in toughness [ 36 ].

In summary, at L temperatures of 800 and 820 °C, IF and fine M/B phases are formed, generating a heterogeneous lamellar structure that enhances toughness. When L is 840 °C or higher, the reduction in IF and the decrease in HAGB density facilitate brittle fracture. Therefore, an optimal L window slightly below  A c3  achieves a balanced combination of strength and toughness.

sections.heading: Effect of tempering temperature
paragraphs: EBSD analysis (Fig.  8 ) shows that the TMCP sample has high KAM and dense LAGBs, reflecting high residual strain and low toughness. T at 400 °C only partially relieves strain, retaining high KAM and limiting toughness improvement. In contrast, T at 500 and 550 °C promotes recovery, reduces KAM and increases grain-boundary tortuosity, improving strain compatibility and suppressing cleavage. Excessive LAGBs are often associated with high KAM, which promotes microcrack formation and reducing toughness [ 37 ]. Thus, toughness depends on coordinated control of KAM and boundary density, not merely increasing HAGBs. It should be noted that precipitation also plays a crucial role in toughness; however, this aspect is beyond the scope of the present work.

The contribution of dislocation, solid-solution, and grain-refinement strengthening was calculated using the equations given in Refs. [ 23 ,  42 ,  43 ], respectively. All material parameters (Hall–Petch coefficient, Taylor factor, shear modulus, and geometrical constants) were selected according to Refs. [ 39 ,  44 ,  45 ]. The computed contributions for various T temperatures are summarized in Table  3 . Table 3 Values of strengthening contribution at various T temperatures No. YS/MPa σ 0 /MPa σ s /MPa σ g /MPa σ p /MPa σ d /MPa L 800 T 350 741 45 75 192 171 405 L 810 T 400 687 45 75 189 244 323 L 810 T 500 756 45 75 185 363 337 L 810 T 550 745 45 75 181 395 303

For comparison, the L 800 T 350  condition was denoted as the reference state (T at 350 °C). The evolution with increasing T temperature (from 350 to 550 °C) reflects the continuous microstructural and mechanical changes dominated by the T process. The  σ p  contribution was back-calculated from Eq. ( 4 ) and used to assess the variation in precipitation behavior. With increasing T temperature, recovery and carbide precipitation proceed. Increased  σ p  compensates for reduced  σ d , keeping strength nearly constant from 350 to 550 °C, while higher T temperatures produce a more uniform microstructure and lower KAM/LAGB density [ 46 ]. T at 500 °C gives the best balance of strength and toughness. Further T may cause carbide coarsening and matrix softening. Thus, T temperature governs dislocation recovery and carbide evolution, and a moderate value (~500 °C) yields the optimal strength–toughness balance.

Overall, the mechanical properties are jointly governed by L and T temperatures: L controls microstructural heterogeneity, whereas T regulates dislocation recovery and carbide evolution. Their synergy defines the final strength–toughness balance, with L 810 T 500  providing the optimal combination of high strength and low-temperature impact toughness.

sections.heading: Effect of dislocation state
paragraphs: The effects of L and T temperatures on  ρ M  and dislocation character were analyzed to clarify their roles in low-temperature toughness. At lower L temperatures (800 and 820 °C), the microstructure primarily consists of M/B and IF. The regions that do not undergo austenitization transform into IF after L treatment, leading to a decrease in  ρ M  [ 13 ]. When the L temperature increases to 840–860 °C, the  ρ M  increases sharply due to intense lattice shearing and dislocation entanglement. At 860 °C (L 860 ),  ρ M  reaches 1.25 × 10 15  m − 2 , exceeding that of the TMCP state (1.16 × 10 15  m − 2 ), whereas lower L temperatures yield  ρ M  of 8.2 × 10 14 –1.04 × 10 15  m − 2 . As discussed in Sect.  4.1 , at low L temperatures, austenite nucleates in alloy-enriched regions and transforms into martensite rich in screw dislocations ( f screw  ≈ 0.56 at L 800 T 350  and L 820 T 350 ) [ 47 ]. In contrast, at higher L temperatures, full austenitization facilitates the formation of bainite with a greater fraction of edge and mixed dislocations [ 48 ]. The variation in dislocation character with T temperature may be related to selective recovery and the formation of cell-wall substructures [ 49 ,  50 ].

Improved toughness relies not only on a moderate reduction in  ρ M  but also on an increased fraction of screw dislocations, which facilitates substructural reconstruction. In the TMCP state, high  ρ M  and low  f screw  (0.399) cause dislocation entanglement and poor toughness. After T at 400 °C, edge dislocations preferentially climb and annihilate, reducing  ρ M  to 5.21 × 10 14  m − 2  [ 51 ]. Because screw dislocations are restricted in climb, they are selectively retained ( f screw  = 0.755), which promotes the formation of fine subgrain boundaries and facilitates crack deflection, thereby increasing toughness to 143 J. L 810 T 500  gives peak toughness with moderate  ρ M  and high  f screw  (~0.67), enhancing cross-slip and strain uniformity, both of which hinder crack propagation and thereby enhance toughness [ 47 ,  52 ,  53 ]. At 550 °C, precipitate coarsening, subgrain growth, and excessive recovery weaken barrier effects and impair plastic compatibility [ 54 ].

The ductile-to-brittle transition in BCC metals is controlled by kink-pair nucleation and the relative mobility of screw and edge dislocations (expressed by the velocity ratio  v s / v e , where  v s  and  v e  are the velocities of screw and edge dislocations, respectively) [ 55 ,  56 ]. The dislocation velocities were calculated using a mobility equation for BCC metals that incorporates kink-pair formation at low temperatures and phonon drag at higher stresses [ 57 ,  58 – 59 ]. Parameters for the calculations are listed in Table  4  [ 56 ,  58 ,  59 ,  60 – 61 ]. To avoid non-physical negative values of the kink-pair nucleation energy Δ G kp , the resolved shear stress ( τ ) was adjusted following Ref. [ 62 ]. An effective mobility factor  β  ( β  = ( f screw v s )/( f edge v e )) was used to represent the influence of L and T on dislocation motion more accurately than the simple  v s / v e  ratio [ 62 ]. The motion of screw dislocations is governed by the kink-pair mechanism, whose efficiency is reflected by  β . A higher  β  enhances Frank-Read source activity, promotes plastic deformation near the crack tip, and thereby improves crack growth resistance. Since all impact tests were performed at −40 °C, temperature-dependent changes in dislocation mobility were minimized. Consequently, variations in  β  arise solely from differences in dislocation character. Figure  15  shows that  β  increases with suitable L and T conditions, indicating enhanced dislocation activity and improved crack resistance. The corresponding low-temperature toughness values are summarized in Tables  1  and  2 . Fig. 15 β (= ( f screw v s )/( f edge v e )) as functions of lamellarization annealing ( a ) and tempering temperatures ( b ) in experimental steel

In summary, the low-temperature toughness results from the combined influence of L and T treatments. Lower L and moderate T temperatures enhance strain compatibility, while excessive dislocation density or over-tempering reduces toughness. Hence, controlling L and T is key to maintaining the strength–toughness synergy, and future work should further elucidate their effects on crack–microstructure interactions.

sections.heading: Conclusions
paragraphs: L temperature determines the phase morphology: partial austenitization at 800 and 820 °C forms a heterogeneous lamellar structure that enhances toughness, whereas higher temperatures (840 °C or higher) homogenize the microstructure and degrade toughness. T temperature regulates dislocation recovery and precipitation: 400 °C leads to insufficient recovery, 500 °C provides the best strength–toughness balance, and 550 °C causes over-recovery and slightly reduces toughness. The combined effects of L and T control both microstructural heterogeneity and dislocation state; under this synergy, the L 810 T 500  condition yields a moderate dislocation density, a high  f screw , and thus the best overall strength–toughness performance.
